quiz.where: Final test, spot-handoff-file, line 433: "It's long, because it copies in the whole 300-line spec, word for word. Spot the mistake."
quiz.problem: The prompt spots the mistake for the reader. It names the copied spec as the cause, which rules out options c and d ("It should keep the spec and…") before any Lesson knowledge comes in. That leaves a two-way choice between a (boil it down) and b (point to it). The c and d feedback just repeat the prompt ("The copied spec is what makes the file long" / "the part that doesn't belong"). The r1 fix that made every option about the spec caused this. Also, 'by its path' is shaky for a colleague on another laptop if the spec isn't in the repo. The SKILL.md says path or URL.
quiz.evidence: Lesson lines 433-441. handoff/SKILL.md:12 says not to duplicate content already in other artifacts (specs, plans, ADRs, issues, commits, diffs) and to reference them "by path or URL instead". Seed `applied` r1: "spot-handoff-file … every option is now about the spec (boil it down, point to it by path [right], keep it and drop suggested skills, keep it and cut the summary)".
quiz.fix:
Describe the file's parts neutrally and let the reader find the one that doesn't belong:

```test spot-handoff-file
Before sending a half-built feature to a colleague, Dev reads the file `/handoff` wrote, as Matt advises. It has a summary of where the work stands and why, a suggested-skills section, `[removed]` where an API key was, and the whole 300-line spec from the repo pasted in. Spot the mistake.
- [ ] The suggested-skills section: the colleague can pick their own Skills.
  > That section is part of every handoff file: it tells the next agent which Skills to load.
- [x] The pasted spec: it should point to the spec in the repo instead.
  > Right. A handoff file refers to specs, tickets and commits by path or link instead of copying them, so it stays short.
- [ ] The removed key: the colleague will need it to run the code.
  > Keys, passwords and personal details are taken out on purpose. The colleague gets their own key another way.
- [ ] The summary of the work: the colleague can read the diff instead.
  > Where the work stands, why, and what comes next are the core of the file. A diff doesn't carry the why.
```
(Visible lengths 70/65/60/65, so the right answer is not the longest.)

quiz.where: Final test, scenario-find-callers, lines 349-353: "need to know which files call `formatServings`. There are about forty candidate files, and all you need is the list of paths."
quiz.problem: This is the body's own subagent example with the function renamed, so it tests recognition, not transfer. The prompt also restates the cheat-sheet cue for the right answer ("only need the answer"). On top of that, distractor a ("read them all here") is a straw man. Nobody reads forty whole files to get a list of callers, because a search returns the paths. So the scenario barely shows why a subagent helps, and a sharp reader sees a as filler.
quiz.evidence: Body line 128: "Use a subagent to find every file that calls `getLessonBySlug`." Cheat sheet line 325: "A big search where you only need the answer | Ask for a subagent". Writing guide, Lessons from the pilot review: "Use a fresh situation … not the body's own example sentence. Don't restate the defining phrase of the right answer in the prompt."
quiz.fix:
Make the job need real reading, and let the reader apply Thariq's test instead of matching a phrase:

```test scenario-find-callers
You're grilling a change to a recipe site. One question turns on whether any of about forty files rounds servings in a way that breaks with fractions, and checking means reading each one. Once you know, you won't look at those files again this Phase. What do you do?
- [ ] Ask the agent to read all forty here, so it knows them firsthand.
  > Forty files of raw code would eat your Smart zone, and you'll never need that text again.
- [x] Have a subagent read them and send back a short report.
  > Right. The reading happens in the helper's own window; only the conclusion lands in yours. Grilling does the same on its own when a question needs a fact.
- [ ] Type `/clear` first, so there's room for the reading.
  > That throws away the grilling to make room for work a helper could do elsewhere.
- [ ] Type `/compact` first, then do the reading.
  > Compacting mid-Phase loses the thread, and the forty reads still land in your window afterwards.
```
(Visible lengths 65/55/51/41.)
